extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legislators, administrative law reformers, and social security / administrative tribunal officials (Canada)
extracted.subtask_description: Recommendations and evaluative criteria for organizing and operating federal social security appeal processes (pre-contentious review, appeal authorities, a new Federal Social Security Tribunal, enforcement, and sanctions) aimed at improving fairness, speed, and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed in decision-making / timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: The appeal and review procedures must be substantially faster — lengthy delays (often years) are unacceptable for claimants and contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report documents typical delays (e.g., initial decisions ~83–90 days; total processes often 2+ years) and concludes that reorganization of the appeal system is urgently required to reduce withdrawals and to secure administrative justice. Proposals elsewhere set specific temporal limits (see 'Reconsideration time limit' and 'Appeal filing time limits').

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-contentious hierarchical review (reconsideration) independent of original decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: Before appealing to an independent authority, claimants should be able to request a non-contentious review by a body higher in the administrative hierarchy than the original decision-maker, and this re-examination should, as far as possible, not be entrusted to the original decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a system fulfills independence, moral authoritativeness, economy, rapidity and fairness. The proposed structure: (1) non-contentious review by a higher administrative body (reconsideration committee); (2) a second, contentious level (administrative tribunal) with judicial-type procedure; both subject to judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and operation of a departmental 'reconsideration' committee
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation within the Department (for CPP benefits) of an 'appeal committee' or 'reconsideration committee' composed and appointed so as to provide hierarchical review distinct from the original decision unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members appointed by the Minister (chosen by assistant deputy minister); membership to include the assistant deputy minister, two Department officials (one a lawyer), and two outside physicians (for disability cases). Two members constitute a quorum, one of whom should be a physician in disability pension cases. The committee's task is to study the file (with exceptional oral explanations permitted). Fact-gathering remains the responsibility of the Disability Evaluation Division and the Appeals Service. Reconsideration should be limited to six months following the initial decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration time limit (six months)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to seek reconsideration by the departmental committee should be limited to a period of six months following the initial decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-year limit under section 83 should be shortened to six months since existing provisions for new evidence already allow further review and the longer limit delays initiation of appeal litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition / consolidation of lower appeal authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplicity of successive appeal levels (e.g., Umpire, Review Committees) should be eliminated where they do more to hinder than to advance administrative justice; a single process of contentious review is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a principle is admitted that appeals arising from federal social security schemes should be adjudicated by a single tribunal, successive levels become superfluous; recommend abolishing the Review Committee and Umpire and making reconsideration-committee decisions directly appealable to the higher appeal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain or adjust effective local boards (Boards of referees) where justified
rubrics_metrics.description: If a lower appeal body demonstrably functions well (quickly and efficiently), it may be retained rather than abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report recommends retaining the unemployment insurance Boards of referees because over decades they have demonstrated satisfactory, quick, and efficient functioning; contrasts these positively with Review Committees that tend to be informal, inexperienced, and slow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve Review Committee composition if retained (Chairmen lawyers, supervised)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Review Committees cannot be abolished, their performance should be improved by appointing lawyer-chairmen and placing them under the supervision of the higher appeal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chairmen should be chosen from a list of lawyers drawn up for each district by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the federal Minister of Justice; Committees (and Chairmen) should be supervised analogous to the supervision proposed for the Boards of referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of a Federal Social Security Tribunal with enumerated exclusive jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a permanent Federal Social Security Tribunal by statute, enumerating its powers and giving it exclusive last-resort jurisdiction over appeals in specified social security areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal should have exclusive last-resort jurisdiction over appeals concerning: Boards of referees decisions (unemployment benefits), Department of National Revenue decisions (unemployment contributions), reconsideration committee decisions (CPP benefits), Minister of National Revenue decisions (CPP contributions for salaried and self-employed), Minister of Revenue of Quebec decisions (QPP contributions), Minister of National Health and Welfare decisions (family allowances, Old Age Security pensions). The report discusses transfer of some powers now with the Tax Review Board and arrangements for conflicts of determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal composition, quorum and hearing arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal should be composed of five to seven members; appeals may be heard by individual members sitting alone, with the Chairman able to reserve important cases for a three-member panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chairman may reserve cases he considers especially important for hearing by himself and two others. The Tribunal should be accessible throughout Canada; consideration should be given to use of assessors if all members are jurists and technical expertise is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that Tribunal members be qualified jurists (with assessors as needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the Tribunal should, as a rule, be qualified jurists by training, with limited exceptions for the Chairman or one/two members; use assessors for technical expertise when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all members are jurists, the Tribunal should add assessors possessing varied technical expertise; however this complicates structure and may require categories/colleges of members for different case types.

rubrics_metrics.name: No charge for appellants' recourse to the Tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellants should not be charged any fee for access to the Tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There should be no charge for appellants' recourse to the Tribunal, consistent with current access to the tribunals it would replace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave to appeal / prior authorization where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether some appeals (e.g., in CPP benefits) should be subject to prior authorization by the Chairman on grounds such as importance of principles or special circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unemployment insurance proposals the Chairman would rule on applications in light of principle importance or special circumstances; note that structure differs between unemployment insurance (Tribunal as second level) and CPP benefits (where Tribunal might be first contentious level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal filing time limits (three months generally; 45 days for unemployment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set a uniform period within which appeals may be lodged: three months for most categories, but 45 days for unemployment insurance appeals where there is an initial Board of referees process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three months suffices for all categories except unemployment insurance benefits, where the existence of the Board of referees may allow shortening the appeal period to 45 days following the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of Tribunal support services (clerk and secretariat roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clerk responsible for physical organization of sittings and file handling, and a secretariat to supervise and guide Boards of referees and prepare a digest of the Tribunal's caselaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Review Committees are maintained under jurist chairmanship, they too should receive supervision and instructions from the Tribunal's secretariat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement policy for recovery of overpayments
rubrics_metrics.description: When overpayments result from administrative mistake, the Department should refrain from forcibly collecting; prefer negotiated repayment, instalments, or write-off where recovery would cause undue hardship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In CPP overpayments by beneficiaries are relatively infrequent and the Department has not generally used civil/criminal sanctions but negotiates reimbursement and may waive recovery to avoid undue hardship. For unemployment insurance overpayments due to administrative mistake, the recommendation is analogous: avoid forcible collection, consider instalment agreements, or write-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles governing sanctions (criminal vs administrative) and need for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify the relation and appropriate uses of criminal and administrative sanctions in social security and tax statutes, including methods of imposition, recovery of penalties, waiver of sanctions, and recourse available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current statutes (e.g., Unemployment Insurance Act section 123) may create offences without wilful intent and allow both administrative and criminal sanctions. The report calls for a comprehensive analysis and a general theory of 'administrative criminal law' covering proportionality, procedures, and recourses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence, moral authoritativeness, economy and fairness as core design desiderata
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal system should be designed to secure independence, moral authoritativeness, economy of procedures and means, rapidity, and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report emphasizes that a simple two-level system (non-contentious hierarchical review followed by contentious tribunal) is capable of fulfilling these requirements and that complexity should not be introduced unless demonstrably advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address imbalance of resources and expertise between administration and claimants
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and reduce the administrative advantage (technical expertise and material means) enjoyed by the administration over claimants to improve fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations to reduce imbalance include developing accessible social security caselaw, encouraging bar interest in social security litigation, and organizing appeal bodies (e.g., outside physicians in reconsideration committees, jurist members of Tribunal) to provide independent perspectives.
